system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 16 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-05-22 16:04:00 to 2179-06-06 16:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis and cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) was admitted for right upper quadrant pain and fever, concerning for recurrent cholangitis. Despite negative blood cultures and an MRCP showing no biliary dilation or acute cholangitis, she was treated with IV meropenem due to clinical signs of infection. Her symptoms improved, liver enzymes trended downward, and she became afebrile. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic therapy, and she was transitioned to ertapenem to complete a 14-day course. Diuretics were restarted, and lactulose was increased for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis. She was discharged home with home health support, instructions to continue all chronic medications, and follow-up with hepatology and for colonoscopy screening.
problems: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with PSC complicated by 
cirrhosis (Childs B, MELD 9) with ascites, hepatic 
encephalopathy, and esophageal varices who presents with 
persistent fevers and RUQ pain while on meropenem for presumed 
acute cholangitis. Patient was treated with both meropenem and 
daptomycin, and spiked fevers through both regimens. 

# Fever of unknown origin:
Patient had been on ertapenem through a PICC for cholangitis as 
an outpatient after being discharged several days before 
presentation. Her blood cultures have never grown bacteria, but 
she responded well in the past to meropenem. She was placed on 
meropenem upon admission and infectious disease was consulted. 
Her PICC line was pulled, but she continued to spike fevers on 
meropenem. ERCP and CT Torso were negative for an infectious 
source, and blood cultures did not grow any bacteria. Infectious 
disease was consulted. Daptomycin was added to her regimen, she 
continued to spike fevers, and meropenem was discontinued. She 
continued to spike fevers through daptomycin, and all 
antibiotics were discontinued. She then remained afebrile for 
several days prior to discharge. Patient was hemodynamically 
stable throughout hospitalization. She was discharged with clear 
instructions to return to the ED if she began having fevers or 
feeling ill again.

# Primary sclerosing cholangitis w/ cirrhosis c/b ascites, HE 
and varices: No signs of HE while hospitalized; continued home 
lactulose and rifaximin. Patient also was continued on home 
ursodiol and hydroxyzine. Diuretics, lasix and spironolactone, 
were initially held in the setting of concern for infection that 
may progress to hemodynamic instability. Diuretics were resumed 
when patient was stable.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you during your hospitalization 
at the ___. You were admitted 
with acute cholangitis. Although you had been on ertapenem as an 
outpatient, this may have not been active against the type of 
bacteria causing the infection. You were trialed on a course of 
meropenem, and continued to have fevers. You had an ERCP and 
imaging done of your abdomen, neither of which showed any source 
of infection. As you know, blood cultures did not grow any 
bacteria as well. You were then started on a medication called 
daptomycin. Because you continued to have fevers on this, all 
antibiotics were stopped. You are being discharged as you have 
stopped having fevers. However, if you begin to have fevers or 
chills again, or feel less well than your normal well self, 
please return to the hospital. Please tell the emergency room 
physicians that they should NOT give you antibiotics until they 
talk with the liver attending. You were given a signed letter 
from Dr. ___ that anybody needs to contact Dr. ___ 
___ starting antibiotics. 

You should continue to follow up with the liver team as an 
outpatient. 

You were also found to have a 5mm lung nodule on CT scan of your 
chest. Because you are very low risk for having a lung cancer, 
you will need a repeat CT scan in one year.  

We wish you the best of luck in your health.

Sincerely,
Your ___ Care Team

meropenem. ERCP and CT Torso were negative for an infectious 
source, and blood cultures did not grow any bacteria. Infectious 
disease was consulted. Daptomycin was added to her regimen, she 
continued to spike fevers, and meropenem was discontinued. She 
continued to spike fevers through daptomycin, and all 
antibiotics were discontinued. She then remained afebrile for 
several days prior to discharge. Patient was hemodynamically 
stable throughout hospitalization. She was discharged with clear 
instructions to return to the ED if she began having fevers or 
feeling ill again.

# Primary sclerosing cholangitis w/ cirrhosis c/b ascites, HE 
and varices: No signs of HE while hospitalized; continued home 
lactulose and rifaximin. Patient also was continued on home 
ursodiol and hydroxyzine. Diuretics, lasix and spironolactone, 
were initially held in the setting of concern for infection that 
may progress to hemodynamic instability. Diuretics were resumed 
when patient was stable.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you during your hospitalization

with acute cholangitis. Although you had been on ertapenem as an

imaging done of your abdomen, neither of which showed any source 
of infection. As you know, blood cultures did not grow any 
bacteria as well. You were then started on a medication called 
daptomycin. Because you continued to have fevers on this, all 
antibiotics were stopped. You are being discharged as you have 
stopped having fevers. However, if you begin to have fevers or

EXAMINATION:  LIVER OR GALLBLADDER US (SINGLE ORGAN)

INDICATION:  History: ___ with PSB acute cholangitis  // eval for CBD dilation

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the abdomen were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal ultrasound dated ___, MRCP dated ___

FINDINGS: 

LIVER: The hepatic parenchyma is coarsened.  Mild nodular liver contours are
noted.  No definite focal liver masses identified.  The main portal vein is
patent with hepatopetal flow.  Small perihepatic fluid is noted.

BILE DUCTS: There is no intrahepatic biliary dilation. The CBD measures 6 mm.

GALLBLADDER: The gallbladder surgically absent.  An echogenic, shadowing
likely stone is seen in the gallbladder remanent, unchanged since the prior
examination.

PANCREAS: Imaged portion of the pancreas appears within normal limits, without
masses or pancreatic ductal dilation, with portions of the pancreatic tail
obscured by overlying bowel gas.

SPLEEN: Normal echogenicity, measuring 17 cm.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  No sonographic evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal
dilatation.
2. Otherwise stable examination from prior, including findings consistent with
cirrhosis and the sequela of portal hypertension including splenomegaly and
ascites.

EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

INDICATION:  ___ female who with past medical history of PSC and
recent cholangitis presents emergency room for evaluation of a fever 102
despite treatment with meropenum.  // evaluate PICC line placement.

TECHNIQUE:  Upright AP view of the chest

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___.

FINDINGS: 

Left PICC tip terminates in the lower SVC.  Cardiac, mediastinal and hilar
contours are normal.  Pulmonary vasculature is normal.  Lungs are clear.  No
pleural effusion or pneumothorax is present.  Clips are noted in the right
upper quadrant of the abdomen.

IMPRESSION: 

Left PICC tip terminates in the low SVC.  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with psc, cirrhosis, with high fevers on abx //
evaluate for intra abdominal abscess, infection w/in lungs

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence: 1) Stationary Acquisition 6.5 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol
= 31.3 mGy (Body) DLP = 15.6 mGy-cm. 2) Spiral Acquisition 6.0 s, 65.9 cm;
CTDIvol = 16.2 mGy (Body) DLP = 1,067.2 mGy-cm. Total DLP (Body) = 1,083
mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to prior from ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Visualized lung fields are within normal limits. There is no
evidence of pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: Macronodular cirrhosis. No focal hepatic lesions are
identified. There is diffuse intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, with
areas of stricturing, similar compared to previous.  The CBD is not dilated. 
There has been prior cholecystectomy.  The main portal vein is patent.  There
is sequelae of portal hypertension with moderate esophageal varices, mild
gastric varices, and moderate retroperitoneal varices.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: Splenomegaly measuring up to 16.7 cm.  Linear hypodensity in the mid
spleen.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram.
There is no evidence of focal renal lesions or hydronephrosis.  The bladder is
incompletely distended, but is grossly unremarkable.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable. Small bowel loops demonstrate
normal caliber, wall thickness, and enhancement throughout.  The colon and
rectum are within normal limits.  Moderate nonhemorrhagic free fluid within
the abdomen and pelvis.  No evidence of organized collection. No
intra-abdominal abscess.

LYMPH NODES: There is no retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy. There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm. Moderate atherosclerotic
disease is noted.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits.

IMPRESSION:


1. New splenic linear hypodensity, likely infarct.  Splenomegaly.
2. Interval worsening of ascites.  No intra-abdominal abscess.
3. Macronodular cirrhosis. Stable appearance of diffuse intrahepatic biliary
ductal dilatation, compatible with provided history of PSC.  Moderate
esophageal and gastric varices.

EXAMINATION:  CT CHEST W/CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ WOMAN WITH CIRRHOSIS AND HIGH FEVER.  ASSESS FOR
INFECTION.

TECHNIQUE:  INSERT SPLIT TORSO CONTRAST

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 6.5 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 31.3 mGy (Body) DLP =
15.6 mGy-cm.
   2) Spiral Acquisition 6.0 s, 65.9 cm; CTDIvol = 16.2 mGy (Body) DLP =
1,067.2 mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 1,083 mGy-cm.
** Note: This radiation dose report was copied from CLIP ___ (CT ABD AND
PELVIS WITH CONTRAST)

COMPARISON:  There no prior chest CT scans available for review.


FINDINGS: 

Supraclavicular and axillary lymph nodes are not enlarged.  Excluding the
breasts which require mammography for evaluation there are no soft tissue
lesions in the chest wall suspicious for malignancy.  Findings below the
diaphragm will be reported separately.

There are no thyroid lesions warranting further imaging evaluation. 
Atherosclerotic calcification is not apparent in head and neck vessels or in
coronary arteries.  Aorta and pulmonary arteries are not enlarged.  Evaluation
of the heart is best with dedicated cardiac imaging.  Severe distention of
azygos vein and tributaries and chest wall venous collaterals is probably due
to systemic shunting from portal hypertension.

Numerous mediastinal lymph nodes are measurable, but only one is
pathologically enlarged, in the prevascular station, 13 mm, 4:  66.

Pericardium is physiologic.  There is no pleural effusion.

There is no pneumonia or interstitial pulmonary abnormality, the only focal
lung lesion of note is a solitary 5 mm wide nodule in the posterior segment of
the right upper lobe, 4:  45.  Tracheobronchial tree is normal to subsegmental
levels.

There no bone lesions in the chest cage suspicious for malignancy.


IMPRESSION: 

No evidence of intrathoracic malignancy or infection.  Solitary sub cm right
upper lobe lung nodule should be re-evaluated with chest CT in 6 months if the
patient is a smoker or has a known extrathoracic malignancy, but if not, in
one year.

Azygos and chest wall venous enlargement due to portosystemic shunting.

RECOMMENDATION(S):   Solitary sub cm right upper lobe lung nodule should be
re-evaluated with chest CT in 6 months if the patient is a smoker or has a
known extrathoracic malignancy, but if not, in one year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of fevers and right upper quadrant pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I just got out of the hospital six days ago with the same thing. I was on ertapenem at home, but then the fever came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had nausea and pain in the same area?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I threw up after eating a muffin in the last hospital — it had gluten. Then I had diarrhea for two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I'm sorry about that. We’ll make sure to avoid gluten. Your ultrasound today shows no bile duct dilation, and your liver looks stable with cirrhosis, but no acute blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I getting these fevers again? It feels just like cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does look like cholangitis, but your blood cultures and urine cultures haven’t grown anything. We’re starting meropenem again because it helped before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But if there’s no bacteria, why give antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Sometimes in cholangitis, cultures don’t grow the bacteria even if infection is present. We treat based on symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC line was removed yesterday. We sent the tip for testing, but it showed no significant growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the line wasn’t infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t appear so. But you’re still spiking fevers, so we’ve consulted infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding daptomycin to your treatment. It covers different bacteria in case meropenem isn’t effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still getting fevers though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning. We’re doing a CT scan today to look for any hidden infection or abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan of your abdomen and chest didn’t show any abscess or pneumonia. Your lungs are clear, but we did see a small 5 mm nodule in your right upper lobe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A lung nodule? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very small and likely not cancer, especially since you’re not a smoker. We recommend a repeat CT in one year to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still having fevers on both antibiotics. All your blood cultures are negative. We’re considering stopping antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a risk, but if there’s no infection, antibiotics won’t help. We’ll watch you closely. If fevers continue, we may need more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’ve been afebrile since we stopped the antibiotics yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? So the antibiotics weren’t helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It seems not. Sometimes fevers in cirrhosis can be from other causes. We’re glad you’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show mild worsening of anemia, but your liver enzymes are improving — ALT and AlkPhos are down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it means your liver is less inflamed. We’re restarting your diuretics today — furosemide and spironolactone — since you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free for two days. We’re planning to discharge you soon if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But what if the fever comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fevers or feel unwell, go to the ER. But tell them not to start antibiotics without calling our liver team first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an ERCP to look at your bile ducts. There might be a narrowing causing repeated inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help prevent future episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If we find a stricture, we can dilate it to improve bile flow and reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ERCP showed long-term narrowing of the common bile duct, consistent with PSC. No dominant stricture, but we did a balloon dilation to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s done now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It may help reduce future cholangitis episodes. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile for five days. Your physical exam shows mild abdominal distension and fluid wave, but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly still feels full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the ascites. We’ve restarted your diuretics, which should help. Continue low-salt diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing discharge plans. You’ll go home with all your usual medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Since cultures were negative and you improved off antibiotics, we’re not continuing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still doing well. We’ll see you in clinic with the liver team next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything specific?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes — if you develop fever, chills, confusion, or severe abdominal pain, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is tomorrow. We’ll send a letter to the ER so they know not to start antibiotics without calling us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That feels safer. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Also, don’t forget the lung nodule follow-up CT in one year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has. Continue all your home meds: lactulose, rifaximin, ursodiol, diuretics, and omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the gluten-free diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Stick to it to avoid celiac flares. And keep taking your thyroid and depression medications too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just stay in touch with your liver team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember — if you feel unwell, go to the ER but insist they call the liver attending before giving antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure they do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re here to help. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — the ERCP balloon dilation of the common bile duct was completed this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember waking up after. I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That should help with bile flow. We’ll monitor for any complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. Home health will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. Keep following up — your health matters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is scheduled for 16:30. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand everything now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check — you’re alert, no pain, vitals stable. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re better. Remember — call your doctor if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel supported. Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis and cirrhosis was readmitted six days after a prior discharge due to recurrent fevers, right upper quadrant pain, and nausea while on outpatient ertapenem for presumed cholangitis. Despite negative blood and urine cultures and no evidence of biliary obstruction on imaging, she was treated initially with meropenem and later daptomycin due to persistent fevers. After failing to respond to antibiotics and remaining afebrile off treatment, all antibiotics were discontinued. An ERCP showed chronic biliary narrowing consistent with PSC, and balloon dilation was performed. Diuretics were held initially but resumed when stable. She remained afebrile, and was discharged home with instructions to avoid antibiotics in the ED without consulting the liver team and to follow up for a repeat CT scan of a 5 mm lung nodule in one year.
